title: Endpoint Denial of Service: OS Exhaustion Flood
shortTitle: Endpoint Denial of Service: OS Exhaustion Flood
summary: Operating system exhaustion targets the kernel layer, where finite tables and self imposed limits sit. The defining property is that the machine does not need to run out of real capacity; it only needs to reach the maximum number of concurrent connections, backlog entries, or state lookups the operating system allows. Two classic families illustrate the mechanism. In a synchronise flood, the attacker sends large numbers of TCP synchronise packets but never completes the three way handshake, so each half open entry occupies a slot in the connection table until it expires, and the service can no longer accept genuine connections. In an acknowledgement flood, packets referring to connections that do not exist are sent in volume, forcing the kernel to search its state table repeatedly and confirm there is no match, which burns processor time and slows every valid flow. Because the resource being consumed is shared with unrelated services, one targeted port can degrade everything else on the host. Detection is kernel and connection level: a spike in half open or synchronise received entries, a growing backlog on listening sockets, unusually high state lookup costs, rises in retransmission or reset counters, and short lived flows without payload. Legitimate traffic that arrives under load completes handshakes and carries payload, whereas attack traffic leaves orphaned state and almost no application data.

beginner.definition: An operating system exhaustion flood attacks the part of the computer that manages resources. It fills up the limited lists the operating system keeps, such as pending connections. The machine may still have plenty of memory, but it cannot accept new work.
beginner.whyItMatters: These attacks can take a service down with surprisingly little traffic compared with a volume flood. Because the limits are shared, other services on the same machine may fail as well. Attack traffic often looks like ordinary connection attempts in basic logs. Understanding the limits helps you choose the right settings and monitoring.
howItWorks: The attacker sends many connection requests to a service that accepts network connections.
The requests are left unfinished, so each one holds a place in a waiting list.
The operating system has a maximum size for that list, which the flood fills.
New genuine connection requests are then refused, even on a fast network.
A second variant sends acknowledgements for connections that never existed at all.
The system searches its whole state table each time, wasting processor time.
beginner.example: Picture a night desk that hands out numbered tickets, with a rack that holds fifty tickets only. Someone takes fifty tickets and leaves without being served. Real guests now arrive to an empty rack and are turned away. The clerk is free and the building is quiet. The limit, not the workload, caused the failure.
takeaways: This sub-technique attacks operating system limits rather than raw bandwidth.
Half open connection counts are the key signal to watch.
Tuning timeouts, backlog sizes and connection limits reduces the impact.

objectives: Explain how this sub-technique differs from service and application exhaustion.
Describe how an unfinished handshake consumes connection table entries.
Explain why acknowledgement floods consume processor rather than memory.
Identify the connection and kernel counters that reveal exhaustion.
Distinguish attack connection attempts from genuine ones in telemetry.
Describe configuration changes that reduce exposure to these floods.
